description: Microsoft AZ-305 (Designing Microsoft Azure Infrastructure Solutions) exam prep, organised by the skill areas: identity, governance & monitoring; data storage; business continuity; infrastructure. Scenario-style 'what do you recommend' cards for architects designing on Azure.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Azure Monitor Metrics vs Logs: when do you recommend each?
notes.back:
Metrics: lightweight near-real-time numbers → dashboards and fast threshold alerts.
Logs: event records in Log Analytics, queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL) → diagnosis and cross-resource correlation.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: You need one query surface over logs from several subscriptions and on-prem servers. What do you recommend?
notes.back: A central Log Analytics workspace, fed by diagnostic settings (platform logs) and the Azure Monitor Agent (guest OS; on-prem via Azure Arc).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: When do you recommend multiple Log Analytics workspaces instead of one?
notes.back: Data residency per geography, different retention or access requirements, separate billing, or strict team isolation. Otherwise one workspace is simpler and cheaper (commitment tiers).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Log Analytics: workspace-context vs resource-context access?
notes.back:
Workspace-context: read access to all data in the workspace.
Resource-context: only logs of resources you have RBAC on, so teams can share one workspace safely.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Which agent should an AZ-305 design specify for VM guest telemetry, and what did it replace?
notes.back: The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA). It replaced the legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA), retired in 2024.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.text: With the Azure Monitor Agent, a {{c1::Data Collection Rule (DCR)}} defines what to collect, how to transform it and where to send it.
notes.extra: DCRs decouple configuration from the agent; associate them with machines manually or via Azure Policy.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Route the Activity Log and resource logs to a third-party security information and event management (SIEM) outside Azure: what do you configure?
notes.back: Diagnostic settings streaming to an Event Hub, which the SIEM consumes.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.text: Diagnostic setting destinations: {{c1::Log Analytics workspace}}, {{c2::Storage account}}, {{c3::Event Hubs}}, or a partner solution.
notes.extra: Workspace = query/alert; Storage = cheap archive; Event Hubs = stream to external tools.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Metric alert vs log alert: latency and cost?
notes.back:
Metric alert: near-real-time (~1 min), cheap to run often.
Log alert: scheduled Kusto Query Language (KQL) query, richer logic but higher latency and query cost.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Which Azure Monitor component holds the notification/automation logic (email, short message service (SMS), webhook, Function, IT service management (ITSM)) so many alert rules can reuse it?
notes.back: An Action Group.
notes.analogy: An alert rule is the smoke detector; the action group is the phone tree it triggers.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: What is Application Insights, and where does its data live?
notes.back: Azure Monitor's application performance management (APM) feature: requests, response times, dependencies, exceptions. Workspace-based App Insights stores data in Log Analytics, queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Security logs must be kept 7+ years, rarely queried, at low cost. What Log Analytics feature do you recommend?
notes.back: Long-term retention (archive) beyond interactive retention; query it on demand with search jobs or restore.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.text: Log Analytics default interactive retention is {{c1::30}} days, extendable to {{c2::2 years}}, with long-term (archive) retention beyond that.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.text: For predictable high-volume Log Analytics ingestion, {{c1::commitment tiers}} (e.g. 100 GB/day) lower the per-GB price in exchange for a fixed daily minimum.
notes.extra: Low or unpredictable volume: stay on pay-as-you-go.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: Which Azure service gives IP flow verify, next-hop analysis, packet capture and network security group (NSG)/VNet flow logs?
notes.back: Network Watcher (regional).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::01 Monitoring & Logging
notes.front: What do you recommend for interactive, parameterized reports combining logs, metrics and Resource Graph data (e.g. post-incident reviews)?
notes.back: Azure Monitor Workbooks. They can be versioned as Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.text: Azure Active Directory is now called {{c1::Microsoft Entra ID}}; tenant and directory concepts are unchanged.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Name two phishing-resistant passwordless methods Entra ID supports.
notes.back: Windows Hello for Business and Fast Identity Online 2 (FIDO2) security keys (also passkeys). Both use device-bound public-key crypto, so there is no shared secret to phish.
notes.extra: short message service (SMS) and voice codes are not phishing-resistant.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Which Entra ID feature enforces 'require multi-factor authentication (MFA) from untrusted networks' or 'block legacy authentication'?
notes.back: Conditional Access: evaluates signals (user, location, device, app, risk) at sign-in and applies grant/session controls.
notes.analogy: A bouncer who checks not just your ID but where you came from, what you're wearing and who you're with.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Entra Connect: which hybrid sign-in method authenticates entirely in the cloud and is the recommended default?
notes.back: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS): a hash of the password hash is synced. Simplest and keeps working if on-prem is down.
notes.extra: Also enables leaked-credential detection in Entra ID Protection.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Entra Connect: when do you choose Pass-through Authentication (PTA) over password hash synchronization (PHS), and what is the cost?
notes.back: When passwords (even hashed) must not leave on-prem. Agents validate against Active Directory (AD) in real time, so sign-in depends on on-prem availability.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Entra hybrid identity: when is federation (AD FS) still justified?
notes.back: Only for requirements the cloud can't meet, e.g. on-prem smart-card/certificate auth or a third-party on-prem multi-factor authentication (MFA) at sign-in. Most complex option.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Entra business to business (B2B) vs External ID (B2C)?
notes.back:
B2B: partner users access your resources as guests with their home credentials.
External ID / B2C: customers sign up to your apps with social or local accounts.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Why recommend a managed identity instead of a connection string or secret?
notes.back: No credential to store, rotate or leak: Entra ID issues tokens to the resource, and access is granted via RBAC.
notes.analogy: Instead of hiding a key under the doormat, the building recognizes the resident's badge.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: System-assigned vs user-assigned managed identity: when do you use each?
notes.back:
System-assigned: lives and dies with one resource.
User-assigned: standalone resource, shareable across many resources, pre-provisionable.
notes.extra: Example: a VM scale set whose instances all need the same Key Vault access → user-assigned.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: No built-in role fits ('restart VMs and read logs, but not create or delete'). What do you recommend?
notes.back: A custom role (Actions / NotActions / DataActions) assigned at the narrowest scope: least privilege.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Key Vault: which permission model do you recommend for new deployments, and why?
notes.back: Azure RBAC (over legacy vault access policies): fine-grained per-secret scope, standard role assignments, Privileged Identity Management (PIM) and audit integration.
notes.extra: Key Vault stores secrets, keys and TLS certificates.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Regulation demands single-tenant, Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 140-2 Level 3 hardware security modules (HSMs) for keys. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Key Vault Managed HSM (dedicated HSM pool, customer has full control).
notes.extra: Key Vault Premium uses multi-tenant HSMs.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Which Entra feature replaces standing admin access with just-in-time, time-bound role elevation?
notes.back: Privileged Identity Management (PIM): eligible assignments must be activated (justification, approval, multi-factor authentication (MFA)) for a limited window.
notes.analogy: A hotel key card that opens the server room only for the hour you booked.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: Legacy apps in Azure need Kerberos/NTLM/LDAP, but you don't want to extend on-prem Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). What do you recommend?
notes.back: Microsoft Entra Domain Services: managed domain controllers synced from Entra ID; no DCs to deploy or patch.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::02 Identity & Access
notes.front: An external auditor needs time-limited read-only access to a subscription. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Invite as an Entra business to business (B2B) guest and give a Privileged Identity Management (PIM) eligible Reader assignment with an expiry: no standing access.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Azure scopes: which level is the billing and quota boundary, and which groups resources by shared lifecycle?
notes.back:
Subscription: billing and scale/quota boundary.
Resource group: resources deployed and deleted together.
notes.extra: Management groups sit above subscriptions to apply policy and RBAC at scale.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Besides billing, what drives subscription boundaries in a large enterprise?
notes.back: Environment separation (prod vs non-prod blast radius), per-subscription limits/quotas, and differing compliance needs per business unit.
notes.extra: The landing-zone pattern: one subscription per workload/environment.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Azure RBAC vs Azure Policy?
notes.back:
RBAC: who can do what (e.g. restart this VM).
Policy: what resources may look like, regardless of who deploys (e.g. only approved VM stock keeping units (SKUs)).
notes.analogy: RBAC is who gets a key to the building; Policy is the building code every renovation must pass.
notes.extra: Allowed SKUs/images: Policy with deny, enforced before creation.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.text: Azure Policy effects: {{c1::deny}} blocks a non-compliant create/update; {{c2::audit}} allows it but flags non-compliance; {{c3::deployIfNotExists}} deploys a missing related resource (e.g. diagnostic settings).
notes.extra: modify adds or changes properties such as tags; existing resources need a remediation task.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Every resource must carry a CostCenter tag. How do you enforce it?
notes.back: Azure Policy: deny if missing, or modify to add or inherit it automatically (remediation for existing resources).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Name two governance uses of a tagging strategy beyond documentation.
notes.back: Cost allocation/chargeback in Cost Management, and scoping automation or policy (e.g. auto-shutdown for Environment=dev).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Why assign a policy initiative rather than many single policies?
notes.back: It bundles related definitions (e.g. a regulatory benchmark) into one assignment that is simpler to manage, version and report on.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Why assign an org-wide rule (e.g. 'no public IPs on VMs') at management-group scope?
notes.back: Assignments inherit downward, so one assignment covers every current and future subscription. Use narrower scopes for workload-specific rules or exemptions.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Azure Blueprints is retiring. What replaces it?
notes.back: Template Specs (versioned Azure Resource Manager (ARM)/Bicep templates) and Deployment Stacks (grouping, lifecycle and deny-assignment locking).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Prevent accidental deletion of a critical resource even by Owners. What do you recommend?
notes.back: A resource lock (CanNotDelete or ReadOnly) at resource, resource group (RG) or subscription scope. It overrides RBAC for everyone until removed.
notes.analogy: A glass case over the fire-alarm button: even the building owner has to lift it off first.
notes.extra: Pitfall: ReadOnly can break operations that use POST (e.g. listing storage keys).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Which service shows compliance against regulatory standards with a secure score and recommended actions?
notes.back: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (regulatory compliance dashboard). Purview Compliance Manager covers broader Microsoft 365 + Azure compliance.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.text: {{c1::Microsoft Entra ID Governance}} combines entitlement management (access packages), access reviews and Privileged Identity Management (PIM) to automate the identity access lifecycle.
notes.extra: An access package bundles groups, apps and sites that users request, with approval and expiry.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Which Entra feature periodically re-confirms that guest users or group memberships are still needed?
notes.back: Access Reviews (part of Entra ID Governance).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.text: The Azure Well-Architected Framework has five pillars: {{c1::Reliability}}, {{c2::Security}}, {{c3::Cost Optimization}}, {{c4::Operational Excellence}}, {{c5::Performance Efficiency}}.
notes.extra: AZ-305 scenarios test whether your recommendation balances these pillars against the stated requirements.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::03 Governance
notes.front: Cloud Adoption Framework vs Well-Architected Framework: difference in scope?
notes.back:
CAF: the organization's whole cloud journey (strategy → manage).
web application firewall (WAF): the design quality of an individual workload.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.text:
{{c1::Azure SQL Database}}: database-scoped PaaS, least management.
{{c2::Azure SQL Managed Instance}}: PaaS with instance features (SQL Agent, cross-database queries), for lift-and-shift.
{{c3::SQL Server on an Azure VM}}: IaaS, full OS control, you patch everything.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: Azure SQL Database: database transaction unit (DTU) vs vCore purchasing model?
notes.back:
DTU: one bundled compute/memory/IO unit, simple.
vCore: choose compute and storage separately, supports Azure Hybrid Benefit; recommended for production.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.text: Azure SQL Database vCore tiers: {{c1::General Purpose}} (remote storage, most workloads), {{c2::Business Critical}} (local SSD, built-in replicas, low latency), {{c3::Hyperscale}} (independently scaling storage to 100+ TB, fast restores).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: A SaaS provider has hundreds of small tenant databases with unpredictable, non-overlapping spikes. How do you control cost?
notes.back: An elastic pool: databases share pooled compute, so one tenant's peak uses capacity others aren't using.
notes.analogy: A shared office printer: nobody prints all day, so one machine serves the whole floor.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: How do you offload read-heavy reporting from a primary Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: Point reports at a read replica: the built-in read scale-out replica (Business Critical/Premium, Hyperscale) or a geo-secondary, via ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: What does an auto-failover group add beyond active geo-replication?
notes.back: A stable listener endpoint and orchestrated (automatic or manual) failover of a group of databases, so apps don't change connection strings.
notes.extra: Replication is asynchronous: an unplanned failover can lose recent writes.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: Azure SQL backups: Point-in-Time Restore vs Long-Term Retention?
notes.back:
PITR: restore to any moment in a short window, for mistakes and corruption.
LTR: weekly/monthly/yearly full backups kept up to 10 years, for compliance.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.text: Azure SQL Database point-in-time restore (PITR) retention defaults to {{c1::7}} days, configurable up to {{c2::35}} days.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: When do you recommend Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL Flexible Server over Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: When the app depends on the open-source engine (PostgreSQL/MySQL code, extensions, tooling) and you still want managed PaaS with zone-redundant high availability (HA).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: What is on by default for every new Azure SQL database, and what threat does it address?
notes.back: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE): encrypts data files, logs and backups at rest, protecting against stolen media or raw storage access.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: A regulated customer must control (and be able to revoke) the keys protecting their Azure SQL data. What do you recommend?
notes.back: transparent data encryption (TDE) with customer-managed keys (BYOK) stored in Key Vault. Revoking key access makes the database inaccessible.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: What detects SQL injection and anomalous access on Azure SQL and alerts admins?
notes.back: Microsoft Defender for SQL (Defender for Cloud): vulnerability assessment + advanced threat protection.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::04 Relational Data
notes.front: One Azure SQL database has hit its tier's write ceiling. How do you scale writes further?
notes.back: Sharding: partition data across many databases by a shard key (Elastic Database tools or app logic). Vertical scaling has a hard limit.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: When do you recommend Cosmos DB over a relational database?
notes.back: Globally distributed, schema-flexible apps: multi-region replication (reads and optional writes) with low-latency service-level agreements (SLAs), elastic horizontal partitioning and tunable consistency.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.text: Cosmos DB consistency, strongest → weakest: {{c1::Strong}} → {{c2::Bounded Staleness}} → {{c3::Session}} (default) → {{c4::Consistent Prefix}} → {{c5::Eventual}}.
notes.analogy: A dial from 'everyone sees the same newspaper instantly' to 'everyone gets the news eventually, in any order'.
notes.extra: Session = read-your-own-writes per client; the usual right answer. Bounded staleness = lag capped by K versions or T time.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: Migrate a MongoDB app to Azure with minimal code change. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB: existing MongoDB drivers connect unchanged.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.text: Azure Storage account services: {{c1::Blob}} (objects, data lake), {{c2::Files}} (managed Server Message Block (SMB)/NFS shares), {{c3::Queue}} (simple async messages), {{c4::Table}} (NoSQL key-value).
notes.extra: New key-value designs usually pick Cosmos DB for Table.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.text: Blob access tiers and minimum retention: Hot (none) → Cool ({{c1::30}} days) → Cold ({{c2::90}} days) → Archive ({{c3::180}} days, offline: hours of {{c4::rehydration}}).
notes.extra: Colder = cheaper storage, more expensive access. Early deletion is charged for the remaining days.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: What does locally redundant storage (LRS) protect against, and when is it still an acceptable choice?
notes.back: 3 synchronous copies in one datacenter: survives disk/rack failure, not a datacenter loss. Fine for reproducible data, cost-driven cases, or apps that replicate themselves.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: high availability (HA) within a region, surviving a datacenter failure, no cross-region replication. Which redundancy?
notes.back: zone-redundant storage (ZRS): synchronous copies across three availability zones in the region.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: geo-redundant storage (GRS) vs read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)?
notes.back: Both replicate asynchronously to the paired region. GRS: secondary readable only after failover. RA-GRS: a read-only secondary endpoint is always available.
notes.extra: Same distinction for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) vs RA-GZRS.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) vs geo-redundant storage (GRS)?
notes.back: Both copy to a secondary region. In the primary, GZRS keeps 3 copies across zones (ZRS), while GRS keeps 3 copies in one datacenter (LRS).
notes.extra: GZRS = highest durability and availability: zone failure and regional disaster covered.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: Foundation for a big-data platform needing a hierarchical namespace, Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) access control lists (ACLs) and Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) compatibility?
notes.back: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2: Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace enabled.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: Lift-and-shift a file server used by Windows (SMB) and Linux (NFS) clients. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Files (Premium for performance), with identity via on-prem Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) or Entra Kerberos to keep share permissions.
notes.extra: Azure File Sync can keep an on-prem cache.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: SAP HANA or high-performance computing (HPC) needs sub-millisecond, high-throughput shared file storage. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure NetApp Files.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::05 Non-relational Data & Storage
notes.front: Compliance requires blob data to be write-once-read-many (WORM). What do you recommend?
notes.back: Immutable storage policies: time-based retention or legal hold on the container or blob version.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::06 Data Integration & Analytics
notes.front: What orchestrates scheduled extract, transform, load (ETL)/ELT pipelines across on-prem and cloud sources?
notes.back: Azure Data Factory (Synapse/Fabric pipelines use the same engine): connectors, visual designer, integration runtimes.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::06 Data Integration & Analytics
notes.front: Data Factory must read an on-prem Oracle database not reachable from the internet. Which component?
notes.back: A Self-Hosted Integration Runtime installed on-prem (or in a virtual network (VNet)). It connects outbound, so no inbound firewall ports are needed.
notes.analogy: An insider who phones out to headquarters, so nobody needs to unlock the front door from outside.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::06 Data Integration & Analytics
notes.front: Synapse dedicated vs serverless SQL pool?
notes.back:
Dedicated: provisioned compute billed hourly, for predictable warehouse loads.
Serverless: pay per TB scanned, for ad hoc queries over data-lake files.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::06 Data Integration & Analytics
notes.front: When do you recommend Azure Databricks over Synapse?
notes.back: Code-first Spark engineering and ML: notebooks, Python/Scala transformations, Delta Lake atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability (ACID) tables. Synapse fits SQL-centric warehousing.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::06 Data Integration & Analytics
notes.front: Detect anomalies in streaming sensor telemetry as it arrives, using SQL-like queries. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Stream Analytics: serverless windowed SQL over Event Hubs / IoT Hub, writing to Power BI, Storage, Cosmos DB, etc.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::06 Data Integration & Analytics
notes.front: Fast ad hoc exploration over huge volumes of time-series and log data?
notes.back: Azure Data Explorer (Kusto Query Language (KQL); the same engine as Log Analytics).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: recovery point objective (RPO) vs recovery time objective (RTO): what does each one drive in a design?
notes.back:
RPO (max data loss, in time) drives backup/replication frequency.
RTO (max downtime) drives failover automation and standby capacity (cold/warm/hot).
notes.analogy: RPO: how far back is your last save point? RTO: how long until you're playing again?

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: What do you recommend for policy-based, application-consistent backup of Azure VMs, on-prem servers and SQL/SAP HANA in VMs?
notes.back: Azure Backup with a Recovery Services vault (MARS agent for on-prem files).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Azure Backup vs Azure Site Recovery?
notes.back:
Backup: point-in-time copies → 'can I get my data back?'
Site Recovery: continuous replication + orchestrated failover → 'can the app keep running?' (far lower recovery time objective (RTO)).
notes.analogy: Backup is a photo album of your house; Site Recovery is a furnished second house you can move into tonight.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Azure-to-Azure VM replication with Site Recovery: what recovery point objective (RPO) is typical, and why?
notes.back: ~30 seconds to a few minutes, because disk writes replicate continuously; no backup schedule can match that.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Which vault redundancy protects the backups themselves against a regional disaster?
notes.back: geo-redundant storage (GRS) on the Recovery Services vault (vs cheaper locally redundant storage (LRS)/ZRS). Set it before protecting items.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Restore an Azure VM backup in the paired region for compliance testing, without a real outage. Which capability?
notes.back: Cross Region Restore, available when the vault uses geo-redundant storage (GRS).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Ransomware with a stolen admin account tries to delete backups. Which Azure Backup features stop it?
notes.back: Soft delete (deleted backups kept ~14+ days) plus Multi-User Authorization via Resource Guard (second approver for critical operations).
notes.extra: Immutable vaults add a lock so retention can't be shortened.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Cross-region disaster recovery (DR): Azure SQL Database vs SQL Server on an Azure VM?
notes.back:
Azure SQL Database: auto-failover groups.
SQL Server on VM: Always On availability groups across regions, or Site Recovery for the whole VM.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Why doesn't geo-redundant storage (GRS)/ZRS protect blobs against accidental deletion, and what does?
notes.back: Redundancy replicates the mistake. Use blob soft delete, container soft delete and versioning.
notes.analogy: Photocopying a letter doesn't help if you shred all copies at once, or if the typo is on every copy.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::07 Backup & Disaster Recovery
notes.front: Design backup retention for both 'restore yesterday's delete' and a 7-year regulation.
notes.back: One policy with daily backups kept ~30 days plus long-term retention of monthly/yearly points for 7+ years.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: Availability set vs availability zones for VMs?
notes.back:
Availability set: fault and update domains inside one datacenter → rack failures.
Zones: separate datacenters in the region → datacenter failure.
notes.analogy: Availability set: servers on different racks and power strips in one building. Zones: servers in different buildings on the campus.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.text: VM service-level agreement (SLA): two or more VMs across availability zones {{c1::99.99%}}; in an availability set {{c2::99.95%}}.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: What do you recommend for a stateless web tier that autoscales and spreads across zones?
notes.back: A zone-redundant Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules (CPU, queue length), behind a Load Balancer or Application Gateway.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) uniform vs flexible orchestration?
notes.back:
Uniform: identical instances from one model, large stateless fleets.
Flexible: mixed sizes and Spot/regular, standard VMs spread across zones/fault domains; recommended for new deployments.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: What high availability (HA) does Azure SQL Business Critical give with no extra setup?
notes.back: An Always On-style replica set (zone-redundant if enabled) with fast automatic failover and a free readable secondary.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: How does Cosmos DB give global users high availability (HA) and low latency?
notes.back: Multi-region replication near users, automatic failover by region priority, and optional multi-region writes so every region accepts writes.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: What are Azure region pairs for in a business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR) design?
notes.back: Paired regions in one geography get sequential platform updates and recovery priority; geo-redundant storage (GRS) and many geo-replication defaults use the pair as DR target.
notes.extra: Newer regions may have no pair; design your own secondary there.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: Global HTTP app: route users to the closest healthy region. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Front Door: global layer 7 (L7) with health-probe failover and latency routing, plus web application firewall (WAF) and caching.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::08 High Availability
notes.front: Single region, compute across zones, needs layer 7 (L7) routing, TLS termination and web application firewall (WAF). What do you recommend?
notes.back: Zone-redundant Application Gateway v2 with WAF (regional L7).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.text: Azure VM series: {{c1::B}} burstable · {{c2::D}} general purpose · {{c3::E}} memory-optimized · {{c4::F}} compute-optimized
notes.extra: Also: N = GPU, L = storage (local non-volatile memory express (NVMe)), M = very large memory (SAP HANA).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: When do you recommend Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) over Azure Container Apps?
notes.back: When the team needs Kubernetes primitives directly (custom controllers/operators, complex networking, StatefulSets) and has K8s skills. Container Apps = containers without running Kubernetes.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Azure Container Instances vs Container Apps?
notes.back:
ACI: run a container (group) on demand, no orchestration.
Container Apps: managed serverless microservices platform with revisions, ingress, Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) scaling and scale-to-zero.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.text: Azure Functions plans: {{c1::Consumption / Flex Consumption}} pay per execution, scales to zero, cold starts · {{c2::Premium}} pre-warmed instances, virtual network (VNet) integration, long runs · {{c3::Dedicated (App Service plan)}} runs on capacity you already pay for.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Code-defined stateful workflow (chaining, fan-out/fan-in, retries, human approval waits)?
notes.back: Durable Functions: checkpoints orchestration state so long-running workflows survive restarts.
notes.analogy: A bookmark in a long book: the function can be put down and picked up exactly where it left off.
notes.extra: Visual, connector-heavy workflows → Logic Apps.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Nightly job on hundreds of parallel nodes, interruptible, cost-minimized. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Batch with a pool of Spot (low-priority) VMs that scales away when done.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Pricing choice: steady 24/7 baseline for 3 years vs interruptible batch work?
notes.back:
Baseline → Reservations (or a Savings Plan for flexibility).
Interruptible → Spot VMs (evictable, deepest discount).
notes.analogy: Reservations are a season ticket; Spot is standby seating: cheap, but you can be bumped.
notes.extra: Cross-cloud discount and eviction details: Cloud Architecture deck.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Compliance needs dedicated physical servers, or licensing is per physical core. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Dedicated Host.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: App Service vs VMs for a classic web app: who handles what?
notes.back: App Service: Microsoft runs OS, patching and runtime; you deploy code/containers. VM: you own all of that; choose it only when App Service can't host the app.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Zero-downtime App Service releases with instant rollback?
notes.back: Deployment slots: deploy to staging, warm up, swap into production; swap back to roll back.
notes.analogy: An understudy rehearses fully in costume backstage, then swaps in between scenes; if it goes badly, the lead steps back on.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::09 Compute
notes.front: Bursty, unpredictable GPU inference load. What compute do you recommend, and why not a fixed VM?
notes.back: Azure ML managed online endpoints, or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) / Container Apps with GPU workload profiles and autoscaling. A fixed GPU VM bills while idle.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: Expose many backend microservices behind one secured, versioned API with rate limits and keys?
notes.back: Azure API Management: gateway with policies (quotas, JSON Web Token (JWT) validation, transforms) and a developer portal.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: Expose a legacy Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) backend to REST/JSON clients without rewriting it?
notes.back: API Management transformation policies (REST ↔ SOAP translation).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.text: Azure messaging: {{c1::Service Bus}} = reliable ordered business messages (queues, topics, sessions, transactions) · {{c2::Event Grid}} = push-based reactive event routing to many subscribers · {{c3::Event Hubs}} = high-throughput telemetry streaming
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: a message is a command someone must process; an event is a notice that something happened.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: Service Bus queue vs topic?
notes.back:
Queue: each message to one consumer (competing consumers).
Topic: a copy to every matching subscription (pub/sub).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: Why put a queue between components instead of synchronous HTTP calls?
notes.back: The buffer absorbs slow or down consumers (queue-based load leveling): no message loss, no cascading failure, and each side scales independently.
notes.analogy: A restaurant's order rail: waiters keep pinning tickets even when the kitchen is slammed.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: IoT telemetry plus device identity, cloud-to-device commands and device twins?
notes.back: Azure IoT Hub. Event Hubs only ingests; it has no device registry or bi-directional control.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: Cut database load for frequently read, rarely changed data?
notes.back: Azure Cache for Redis as a cache-aside layer (also session state).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::10 Application Architecture
notes.front: Central feature flags and non-secret config across microservices?
notes.back: Azure App Configuration, referencing secrets that stay in Key Vault.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.text: Cloud Adoption Framework phases: {{c1::Strategy}} → {{c2::Plan}} → {{c3::Ready}} → {{c4::Adopt}} (migrate / innovate), with Govern and Manage running throughout.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: What is a landing zone, and why build it before migrating at scale?
notes.back: The pre-built, governed environment (subscriptions, network, identity, policy, monitoring) workloads land in, so every migrated workload inherits controls from day one.
notes.analogy: Laying roads, water and power before houses go up, instead of digging up every garden later.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.text: Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) migration strategies: {{c1::Rehost}} (lift and shift) · {{c2::Refactor}} (small changes to fit PaaS) · {{c3::Rearchitect}} (redesign for cloud-native) · {{c4::Rebuild}} (rewrite) · {{c5::Replace}} (switch to SaaS)

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: Discover and assess on-prem servers (readiness, right-sizing, cost) before migration?
notes.back: Azure Migrate (appliance-based discovery and assessment, hands off to migration tools).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: Check an on-prem SQL Server for compatibility blockers before moving to Azure SQL?
notes.back: An assessment tool: classically Data Migration Assistant (DMA); Microsoft now steers to Azure Migrate / Arc-based SQL assessments.
notes.extra: Exam answers may still name DMA for assessment and Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) for the move.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: Which service performs online (minimal-downtime) database migration into Azure SQL, Managed Instance or Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS): offline cutover or online continuous sync.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: Petabytes of data to Blob Storage and the network is the bottleneck?
notes.back: Azure Data Box (or Data Box Heavy): ship a physical appliance.
notes.analogy: Never underestimate the bandwidth of a truck full of disks.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: Scripted, repeatable file transfers to Blob/Files in a pipeline?
notes.back: AzCopy.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::11 Migration
notes.front: Migrate Windows file servers preserving access control lists (ACLs), with a cutover that takes over the old server name?
notes.back: Storage Migration Service (Windows Admin Center).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: virtual private network (VPN) Gateway vs ExpressRoute for hybrid connectivity?
notes.back:
VPN: Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) over the internet; cheap, variable latency.
ExpressRoute: private circuit via a provider (or ExpressRoute Direct); higher bandwidth, predictable latency, service-level agreement (SLA).
notes.analogy: VPN: an armoured car on the public motorway. ExpressRoute: your own private rail line.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: What do you recommend as a backup path for an ExpressRoute circuit?
notes.back: A site-to-site virtual private network (VPN) as failover: the circuit is still one physical path.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.text: virtual network (VNet) peering is {{c1::non-transitive}}: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C through B.
notes.analogy: A friend of a friend is not automatically your friend.
notes.extra: Full mesh grows as n(n−1)/2 links, so at scale use hub-spoke or Virtual wide area network (WAN).

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Hub-spoke topology: what lives in the hub, and what is the benefit?
notes.back: Shared services (virtual private network (VPN)/ExpressRoute gateways, Azure Firewall, DNS) in the hub; workloads in peered spokes. Central inspection and no duplicated gateways.
notes.analogy: An airline hub: spokes fly through one airport where security screening happens once.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Dozens of branches and virtual networks (VNets) need any-to-any connectivity without hand-building hub-spoke. What do you recommend?
notes.back: Azure Virtual wide area network (WAN): managed hubs, software-defined wide area network (SD-WAN) branch integration, transitive routing.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Force all spoke internet egress through Azure Firewall in the hub. How?
notes.back: A user-defined route (UDR) on each spoke subnet: 0.0.0.0/0 → next hop = firewall's private IP, overriding the default internet route.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: network security group (NSG) vs Azure Firewall?
notes.back:
NSG: free, distributed L3/L4 filter on a subnet/NIC.
Azure Firewall: central managed L3–layer 7 (L7) firewall (fully qualified domain name (FQDN) filtering, threat intel), usually in the hub. Complementary.
notes.analogy: NSGs are locks on each room door; Azure Firewall is the security desk in the lobby that inspects everyone leaving the building.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Protect a public web app from SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS). What do you recommend?
notes.back: A Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway (regional) or Front Door (global), using Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) rule sets.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: When do you recommend paid Azure distributed denial of service (DDoS) Protection over the free infrastructure protection?
notes.back: Internet-facing production apps needing adaptive tuning per app, attack telemetry, cost protection and the DDoS Rapid Response team.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.text: Azure load balancing: {{c1::Load Balancer}} = layer 4 (L4), regional · {{c2::Application Gateway}} = layer 7 (L7), regional (web application firewall (WAF), TLS offload, path routing) · {{c3::Front Door}} = L7, global edge (WAF, caching) · {{c4::Traffic Manager}} = DNS-based, global, any protocol

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Why choose Traffic Manager over Front Door for global failover?
notes.back: It works at the DNS level, so it handles non-HTTP protocols (game servers, custom TCP). Front Door only proxies HTTP(S).
notes.analogy: Traffic Manager is a phone directory that tells you which branch to call; Front Door is a receptionist who takes the call and connects it.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Service endpoint vs private endpoint for reaching a PaaS service from a virtual network (VNet)?
notes.back:
Service endpoint: PaaS firewall trusts your subnet, but the service keeps its public endpoint.
Private endpoint: private IP inside your VNet, reachable from on-prem too. Preferred.
notes.analogy: Service endpoint: the shop's public door with your name on the guest list. Private endpoint: the shop opens a counter inside your own office.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: What must accompany a private endpoint so clients resolve the PaaS name to the private IP?
notes.back: A Private DNS zone (e.g. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) linked to the virtual network (VNet). Otherwise names resolve to the public IP.
notes.extra: On-prem clients need a DNS forwarder / Private Resolver pointing at it.

notes.deck: AZ-305 Solutions Architect Expert::12 Networking
notes.front: Chatty VM-to-VM traffic needs lower latency and less CPU overhead. What do you enable?
notes.back: Accelerated Networking (SR-IOV): bypasses the host virtual switch.
